lead: The uterus turns inside out, almost always in the 3rd stage of labour. About 1 in 2000–3000 deliveries; maternal death up to 15% if not treated fast.
f: Classification

1st degree: fundus in the cavity, not past the cervix · 2nd: through the cervix, in the vagina · 3rd: to or beyond the vulva · 4th: uterus and vagina turned out · Incomplete = 1st, 2nd · complete = 3rd, 4th · Acute < 24 h (most) · Subacute 24 h – 4 wk · Chronic > 4 wk (often a fundal fibroid polyp)

sc: Fundus past the cervix but not the vulva → Second degree (incomplete)

f: Aetiology

Mismanaged 3rd stage: cord traction before separation, no counter-traction · Fundal pressure (Credé) on a relaxed uterus · Fundal placenta, short cord · Atony · Placenta accreta, fundal fibroid · Uterine anomaly, previous inversion
Pathophysiology

Relaxed fundus (placental site) dimples in · Cord traction or fundal push pulls it down · Cervix closes as a constriction ring; the fundus swells · Traction on ovaries, tubes and peritoneum: vagal (neurogenic) shock with bradycardia, plus bleeding
Clinical features

Severe pain in the 3rd stage · PPH in about 94% · Shock out of proportion to the blood loss, slow pulse · Abdomen: fundus absent or a cup at the top · VE: purple-red mass in the vagina or at the vulva, placenta may be on it

sc: Cord pulled hard, pulse 52, BP 70/40, little bleeding, red mass at the vulva → Acute inversion, vagal shock

f: Investigations
Diagnosis is clinical: replace first · At the same time: CBC, coagulation, cross-match 4–6 units · Ultrasound only if unclear (subacute, chronic)

tr: Ultrasound before replacing an acute inversion wastes the minutes that matter

f: Differential diagnosis

Atonic PPH: soft fundus felt, shock matches the loss · Uterine rupture: shock with a fast pulse, scar, labour pain · Amniotic fluid embolism: cyanosis, fits, then bleeding; uterus in place · Mass in the vagina with a normal fundus: fibroid polyp, prolapse, vaginal haematoma
Management: the drill
Call help · Replace at once, everything else in parallel: the ring tightens every minute · Leave the placenta on until the uterus is back · IV lines, fluids, blood

tr: Removing the placenta first makes the raw bed bleed torrentially

f: Methods of replacement

Johnson manoeuvre: palm on the fundus, push up through the cervix toward the umbilicus; the part out last goes in first; hold 3–5 min · Relax the ring: terbutaline 0.25 mg SC, MgSO₄ 4 g IV over 15 min, or GA with a volatile agent · O'Sullivan (hydrostatic): 2–5 L warm saline into the sealed vagina; exclude rupture first · Huntington (laparotomy): clamps on the round ligaments, pull up step by step · Haultain (laparotomy): posterior incision through a tight ring

sc: Ring tight, uterus will not go up → Terbutaline or GA, then Johnson
Ring too tight at laparotomy → Haultain incision

f: After replacement

Stop tocolysis, start oxytocin 40 IU in 500 mL over 4 h; fist in the fundus until it contracts · Then manual removal of the placenta in theatre; check for tears · Antibiotics, transfusion · Watch for re-inversion and PPH

sc: Uterus replaced → Oxytocin infusion; stop the tocolytic

f: Subacute and chronic inversion
Ring fixed, uterus swollen: treat shock and infection first · Replacement under GA, usually at laparotomy (Huntington, Haultain) · Chronic: look for a fundal fibroid polyp; hysterectomy if necrotic

sc: 6 weeks after a home birth, red mass in the vagina, no fundus, a cup at the top → Chronic inversion: laparotomy (Haultain)

f: Prevention

Active 3rd stage: oxytocin 10 IU IM · Controlled cord traction only after signs of separation, with counter-pressure above the pubis · No Credé, no pulling on a relaxed uterus · Previous inversion: it can recur; deliver in hospital
